0fb21836-e5e1-51dd-ab52-da180f9f90b6.name: Oud
0fb21836-e5e1-51dd-ab52-da180f9f90b6.short_description: The oud is the Arabic word for a lute, a pear-shaped instrument with a short fretted kneck and six sets of double strings. It is played with a plectrum, usually made of trimmed eagle feather, and has a deep, mellow sound. The word 'lute' in English comes from the Arabic "al-oud", via the Spanish word for the instrument, "laúd".
0fb21836-e5e1-51dd-ab52-da180f9f90b6.holder: Lebanese National Higher Conservatory of Music
0fb21836-e5e1-51dd-ab52-da180f9f90b6.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Hassan El Masri, Remy Nader

0fc10372-d4f9-5ea4-a201-8d7651379544.name: Arabian shawm (*zamr*)
0fc10372-d4f9-5ea4-a201-8d7651379544.short_description: Woodwind instrument made of boxwood, with a flared bell. Thumb hole with seven finger holes. The short and wide double-reed (1.5cm wide) is attached to a copper staple, and inserted into a pirouette in form of a bone plaque (4.5cm in diameter); four small chains made of white metal are suspended from it.

109ed34a-507a-5652-bb30-736569eca0ac.name: Drum
109ed34a-507a-5652-bb30-736569eca0ac.short_description: Small round drum, pointed on the bottom, covered on the top with leather, and fastened with a linen rope. It was played with a wooden stick to create special sounds of music, and it was used during the Muslim holy month of Ramadan to wake up people to eat (*suhur*) before sunrise. Some people used to volunteer to go around before dawn to wake people up during Holy Ramadan, reflecting community spirit.

14d25094-56e3-5812-add7-3c7c717c6829.name: Mijwiz
14d25094-56e3-5812-add7-3c7c717c6829.short_description: The *mijwiz*, meaning "double" in Arabic, is a common instrument in traditional Lebanese music. It is a type of reed clarinet, played by breathing slowly through a circular aperture at the end of the instrument, and covering the holes down the body of the instrument with your fingers in order to create different notes.

15744871-f248-53cf-8b39-f21c90b970bd.name: Goblet drum with label of the Vienna World's Fair 1873
15744871-f248-53cf-8b39-f21c90b970bd.short_description: The 1873, the Vienna World´s Fair provided substantial momentum for the popularisation of oriental style and fashion in middle-class society. At the same time, domestic handicrafts were revitalised by drawing inspiration from the ample supply of exotic materials. Everything is "Orientalised," from the timeless children's fork to simple chairs. The Oriental Museum, founded in 1875, was intended to boost trade with the Orient; its basic inventory of arts and crafts was taken from the World‘s Fair. Eleven years later, the Oriental Museum was renamed the ‘Austrian Commercial Museum'. When Europe began to flood the market with domestically produced and Orientalised articles, the exotic flavour of the Orient had already lost its magic. At the turn of the century, a large portion of the collection became part of the ethnographic department of the Imperial and Royal Court Museum of Natural History (today, Weltmuseum Wien). In 1925, the Austrian Commercial Museum was dissolved.
15744871-f248-53cf-8b39-f21c90b970bd.method_for_datation: Original label in French: "Exposition Universelle de 1873. Vienne. Empire Ottoman. No. du Groupe 15, No. du Catalogue 5."

45aa6bbe-dbdf-5f6e-b23b-222901c8201e.name: *Cümbüş* (embroidered)
45aa6bbe-dbdf-5f6e-b23b-222901c8201e.short_description: This a music instrument developed in the early 20th century and used for folk dances played at engagements, weddings and other traditional celebrations.

4ff776a6-3eb5-5f3e-935c-a64b779f2d12.name: Arabian *qānūn*
4ff776a6-3eb5-5f3e-935c-a64b779f2d12.short_description: Trapezoid-shaped soundbox made of black painted wood, decorated with three gilt roses with foliage; as is typical for this instrument, the lower part is covered with parchment. The bridge rests on four feet and holds treble-chord gut strings (originally there were 19) attached to wooden pegs.
4ff776a6-3eb5-5f3e-935c-a64b779f2d12.obtention: The item belonged to the collection of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria-Este

529b4a95-033c-586c-b6c2-ba606e63c4aa.name: Buzuq
529b4a95-033c-586c-b6c2-ba606e63c4aa.short_description: The word *buzuq* comes from Turkish. *Bashi-buzuq* for example, literally meaning 'burnt head', was one of the nicknames given to the Ottoman troops. The *buzuq* is of hybrid origin and thus is considered neither a traditional Arabic instrument nor a traditional Turkish instrument. Used for *dabke* music, the instrument was originally associated with the traveller communities in Lebanon. It consists of a long, fretted neck with four sets of double strings, and is played with a plectrum.

5384b8df-a79b-54a7-bdbf-0c4918314519.name: Qanun
5384b8df-a79b-54a7-bdbf-0c4918314519.short_description: The *qanun* is a traditional instrument of the Middle East, whose name in Arabic also means "rule, principle or norm". It has a range of three octaves, and today it is made with nylon or PVC strings are stretched over a single bridge, poised on fish-skins on one end, and attached to tuning pegs on the other. Turkish models have 26 sets of triple strings. It rests on the player's lap and is played by plucking, either with the player's fingernails or with two tortoise-shell plectrums.

57c4d2b9-c19a-5dbd-bbac-17570a133ace.name: Lyre (*tanga*)
57c4d2b9-c19a-5dbd-bbac-17570a133ace.short_description: In Egypt's Western Desert, at the oasis of Siwa, Sliman Sheib Said wants to craft a five-stringed lyre. This is not a typical instrument for this oasis, where flutes, drums, tambourines, and the rhythmic clapping of hands dominate the music. Such lyres are at home in Nubia or the Sudan. In the 1950s, the first transistor radios go into serial production in Europe and by the  1970s, affordable transistor radios became popular in the oasis. Men dance and sing to radio music. Then, the Walkman and iPods bring the era of the battery-operated transistor radios to an end. Throw them away! From the casing of such a discarded portable transistor radio, Sliman creates his desired musical instrument. In 1993 an ethnologist documents the transformation of the material culture in the oasis. One evening, as she is hanging out in the "East-West Restaurant", Sliman passes by with his lyre. He declares himself ready to sell her his lyre, but only on the next day, after the evening party in the palm garden, to which he is making his way.

61aa5d2d-8152-5e70-a44f-0e91a3eb81dc.name: North-African lute (*kuitra*)
61aa5d2d-8152-5e70-a44f-0e91a3eb81dc.short_description: The lute has a shell made of nine ribs of deciduous wood. The soundboard is of stained softwood with the soundhole resembling a tree of life. The neck of softwood has a slanting pegbox. The carved bridge has black varnish, and four double chords.

6361ef20-5b25-59b2-bd56-7f7ed9244291.name: Reed pipe
6361ef20-5b25-59b2-bd56-7f7ed9244291.short_description: A pair of blank reeds opened from both sides, of moderate thickness. Each has six holes on the surface attached together with a type of gum. Playing the *mijwiz* requires some ability because it is played by blowing into both reeds at the same time and pushing the air strongly with the cheeks. Shepherds used to play it while taking their flocks of sheep and goats to graze. It is a popular traditional musical instrument in the Middle East.

6faa2e57-f95c-52d9-a61f-402154b53322.name: Organ Made in Tunis by the Italian Firm Cesare Trionfo and Exhibited in Milan
6faa2e57-f95c-52d9-a61f-402154b53322.short_description:
Cesare Trionfo was a child when he migrated with his family to Tunisia from Livorno in 1855. He became a trader, and in 1886 he started trading musical instruments. In Tunis, he later also started a shop that made musical instruments such as this organ. Trionfo promoted the construction of the theatre Politeama Roissini, which he co-owned.  
This organ was exhibited in Milan for the 1906 international exhibition. The organ is a traditional Italian musical instrument. This one has decorative elements taken from Arab architecture.
6faa2e57-f95c-52d9-a61f-402154b53322.author: Giulia Barrera

71d1bb15-43f9-5e5d-8a1d-7e157badf90e.name: Daff
71d1bb15-43f9-5e5d-8a1d-7e157badf90e.short_description: The *daff*, also known as the *rikk*, is a popular instrument similar to a tambourine. It is made of a round wooden frame, covered on one side with goat or fish skin. Pairs of metal discs are set into the frame to produce a jingling sound when the instrument is struck. It is used to set the rhythm in many traditional Arabic songs, particularly during purely instrumental performances.
71d1bb15-43f9-5e5d-8a1d-7e157badf90e.holder: Lebanese National Higher Conservatory of Music
71d1bb15-43f9-5e5d-8a1d-7e157badf90e.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Hassan El Masri, Remy Nader

79b8cfeb-10a3-540e-9629-97e22633b9d0.name: Lyre (*tambura*)
79b8cfeb-10a3-540e-9629-97e22633b9d0.short_description: A three, four, five or six-stringed lyre whose round sound box is covered with stretched goatskin with two openings called eyes (Arabic *‘ain*). Protruding diagonally from the sound box are two wooden posts that are connected by crossbars at various heights and roughly form a trapezium. The wooden posts and the crossbars are wrapped with coloured ribbons, strings of pearls and brushes, and decorated with shells and amulets. The *tambura* is the most important instrument and is considered to be inspired by the *asyad*, masters who speak with the possessed. During the *zar* ceremonies (a form of dance therapy which displays a few points of connection with formal Islam) of North and East Africa the *tambura* is placed on a sacrificial table (*kursi*) with a set of indispensable items: candlesticks, flowers, food products and incense.

7c628f29-8443-5e2e-8926-884729f02df3.name: Legged violin
7c628f29-8443-5e2e-8926-884729f02df3.short_description: The Violin was not a popular instrument in 16th century except among patrons of taverns. In the early 19th century, musicians used both types of violin – the legged violin and the sine or "chest" violin – but the sine violin disappeared afterwards. The legged violin has a cylindrical body with a relatively long handle. The cut body is made of coconut shell and covered with leather.

8951f6af-b5d8-564b-983b-9fd818e52be8.name: Tabla
8951f6af-b5d8-564b-983b-9fd818e52be8.short_description: The *tabla*, also known as the *durbakke*, is a small hand drum very common in traditional Arabic music. It is shaped like a vase, and is covered at the top with goat skin. *Tabla*s are often beautifully decorated, with metal, bone inlay, or paint.

92b4c27b-fe74-52f2-a879-77344c6edb4d.name: Virginal
92b4c27b-fe74-52f2-a879-77344c6edb4d.short_description:
The maker of this glass-covered virginal is still unknown, and it has no known parallel among keyboard instruments, making it highly unique.  
  
The majority of the faces of the instrument are either enamelled or adorned with lamp-worked rods (tooled and fused in the open flame of a lamp or torch), whorls and florets. However, the inner lid is set with 18 panels which depict scenes from the Roman poet Ovid's work *Metamorphoses*. These intricately and exquisitely detailed scenes are framed within scrolling borders and each is labelled with the name of the characters who appear in the 25 books that constitute the poem. Included are Acteon, the hunter who, after catching sight of the goddess Diana bathing was transformed into a stag and killed by his own hounds.  
  
The uniqueness of the virginal has meant it has been associated with a glass virginal that was described as in the possession of Elizabeth I at Hampton Court. A German traveller named Paul Hentzner wrote in 1598 of 'a musical instrument made all of glass except the strings'. However, other contemporary descriptions of instruments at Hampton Court describe them being encrusted with jewels and inscribed with the Queen's cypher, which this instrument is unfortunately lacking.
92b4c27b-fe74-52f2-a879-77344c6edb4d.bibliography:
Jervis, Simon, "Glass reliefs at Schloss Ambras and the Victoria & Albert Museum", *Burlington Magazine*, Vol. CXXXII (1990): 351-353.  
Thornton, Peter, *Musical Instruments as Works of Art*, London: HMSO, 1968: fig. 21.
92b4c27b-fe74-52f2-a879-77344c6edb4d.author: Simon Spier
materials: A virginal in a stamped and gilt leather case, decorated internally with eighteen scenes from Ovid's Metamorphoses lampworked in glass relief.

a0b0c8e0-a3e5-55bb-9e5b-4ddf40ae3944.name: *Kemençe*
a0b0c8e0-a3e5-55bb-9e5b-4ddf40ae3944.short_description: This four-stringed musical instrument has a facetted wooden body overlaid with tortoiseshell and lavishly inlaid with floral scrolls and arabesques executed in mother-of-pearl. In Ottoman culture the *kemençe*, which is bowed vertically while resting on the player’s knee, was one of the main classical instruments used.
keywords: Musical instruments; inlay; floral decoration; arabesque

b6227f02-1142-5b04-b3af-734ad8573ce6.name: Drums
b6227f02-1142-5b04-b3af-734ad8573ce6.short_description: The two drums are part of the flourishing tradition of enamelled ceramic in Fez, in production since the Middle Ages. Cobalt blue and white decorations identify Fez products dating to the second half of the 19th century. The drums belong to the ethnographic collections of the Pigorini Museum founded between the 19th and the 20th century. The origins of scientific activity and conservation of Museo Nazionale Preistorico Etnografico "Luigi Pigorini" in Rome, can be traced back to the foundation in 1875 of the "Royal National Museum of Prehistory and Ethnography in Rome" within the buildings of the Roman College.

b8a6b459-47fa-5a6f-a12b-76e7e938843b.name: *Parmak cura* (little *cura*)
b8a6b459-47fa-5a6f-a12b-76e7e938843b.short_description: The *Cura* is an instrument used by Yörüks (nomads). It is the smallest type of *bağlama* and is usually 55-60cm in length. It generally has three, four, five or six strings and is played either with a quill or the fingers. It is suitable for dynamic dance performances.

ce544eac-b951-5657-9a7f-51c32a2f26c6.name: Drum.
ce544eac-b951-5657-9a7f-51c32a2f26c6.description:
A cast bronze drum with a wide mouth, a body that narrows toward the bottom, and a flat base. The exterior of the rim of the drum has four handles and a row of large pegs for attaching the drumhead. The body is covered with three friezes of engraved decoration.  
  
The main frieze consists of arabesques above which is set an inscription in monumental *kufic* script whose letters' verticals terminate in dragon and human heads, the latter in pairs. The dragon heads closely resemble those on the door knockers of the Ulu Cami (Great Mosque) in Cizre. The second frieze consists of spiral arabesques, while the lower frieze is made up of plaited bands with stylised palmettes. The style of the dragon heads and arabesques is further evidence for a provenance of the Artukid region in the AH 7th / AD 13th century.
ce544eac-b951-5657-9a7f-51c32a2f26c6.short_description: This cast bronze drum was used as a ceremonial drum in army bands. It is a rare masterpiece of AH 7th- / AD 13th-century Artuqid metalwork with its calligraphic script and floral and figurative decoration.
ce544eac-b951-5657-9a7f-51c32a2f26c6.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
ce544eac-b951-5657-9a7f-51c32a2f26c6.method_for_datation: The human- and dragon-headed *kufic* calligraphy that adorns the bronze drum, although it is unparalleled, is related in many ways to works from the beginning of the 7th / 13th century (for example, a footed bowl from Napolitan Pinacoteca, which is dated to the first quarter of the 13th century and attributed to Iran; and a ewer from the British Museum, considered a work of the Khurasan school). These similarities, as well as the fact that it was found at Diyarbakır in southeastern Anatolia, allow us to date the drum to the period of the Artuqid Melik Nasireddin \[Nasr al-Din\] Mahmud (r. 596–618 / 1200–22).
ce544eac-b951-5657-9a7f-51c32a2f26c6.method_for_provenance: In the monumental *kufic* script on the body, those letters which occur in pairs end with crowned human heads, while single letters end in dragon heads. These can be seen to resemble the dragon heads on the door knockers of the Ulu Cami (Great Mosque) in Cizre. This is evidence that the bronze drum was made in Artukid region during the same period.
ce544eac-b951-5657-9a7f-51c32a2f26c6.obtention: The object was transferred from Diyarbakır to the Topkapı Palace Museum, and then in AD 1951 to the Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.

dff63501-6388-5281-9baf-bb1a3d253e7f.name: Rababa
dff63501-6388-5281-9baf-bb1a3d253e7f.short_description: Four pieces of wood formed into a rectangular shape; the top and bottom are covered with animal skin and joined with goat’s intestines. The rababa is played with a bow consisting of an arched stick with horse hair. The rababa is a musical instrument widely used in the Bedouin tradition. Music played in communal setting is an essential part of the traditions in Bedouin communities for leisure at communal gatherings.

f0a22720-4486-5cd9-b830-526d7c53d494.name: Kettledrum.
f0a22720-4486-5cd9-b830-526d7c53d494.description:
The kettledrum is of hemispherical form and has a flat base. In the plain zone below the upper edge there are four rectangular loops with 16 protuberances in between serving to fix the drumhead, which is now missing. The decorated surface of the kettledrum consists of two zones. Both show medallions alternating with oblong panels on a background of a Y-pattern. The panels of the central zone contain a bold *naskhi* inscription against a background of arabesques. The text consists of nine nouns expressing praise and good wishes, without referring to the owner or mentioning his name. The medallions are filled with arabesques and whirling motifs. The oblong panels in the zone towards the base of the kettledrum show a *kufic* inscription of unknown content. The eagles with heads turned to the left and claws grasping the tips of the wings show the typical form of this bird used as an emblem by the Mamluk amirs. The emblem is repeated twice on the flat base on either side of a rectangular loop.  
This kettledrum was probably used in falconry to call the falcon back to the owner.
f0a22720-4486-5cd9-b830-526d7c53d494.short_description: Kettledrum of hemispherical form and with a flat base. The loops below the upper edge served to fix the drumhead. It is decorated with panels containing an inscription and medallions filled with arabesques and whirling motifs. It was probably used in falconry to call the falcon back to its owner.
f0a22720-4486-5cd9-b830-526d7c53d494.dates: Hegira first half of 8th century / AD first half of 14th century.
f0a22720-4486-5cd9-b830-526d7c53d494.method_for_datation: Lamm (see Bibliography) dated the kettledrum to the first half of the 8th / 14th century.
f0a22720-4486-5cd9-b830-526d7c53d494.method_for_provenance: As a place of manufacture Lamm (see Bibliography) suggests Cairo, but he does not give a reason.
f0a22720-4486-5cd9-b830-526d7c53d494.obtention: The kettledrum was bought from the art collector Carl Robert Lamm by the Royal Armoury in 1922. In 1899, Lamm acquired it from F. R. Martin who had bought the kettledrum in Cairo during his journey through Egypt and Turkey in 1895–6.

f8c2bcec-57eb-5f11-8bfe-5d3461e46436.name: Lute
f8c2bcec-57eb-5f11-8bfe-5d3461e46436.description:
Plucked instrument with four double orders. The headstock is inlaid with silver motifs. It has eight round pins decorated with flowers which end in bone buttons. The nut is also made of bone. The fingerboard is adorned with marquetry and inlay work and has been partially restored; it has no frets.  
The lid is decorated with a quite flamboyant pierced rosette. The bridge is made of bone and wood with stars decoration. The wavy tailpiece is made of wood. The neck is decorated with marquetry in two colours forming a zigzag. The soundboard is concave and consists of eleven staves.
